changes.after: A range for the average response answers a different question from a range for one future observation.

before: predict.lm with interval = "confidence" estimates uncertainty about the conditional mean response. interval = "prediction" additionally accounts for variation in one future observation under the fitted model, so it is wider here. Both depend on assumptions, not just successful software execution.

newdata supplies predictor values in a data frame. Its x = 3 is inside the observed range 1..5. Predictions far outside that range can be scientifically unreliable even if R returns a number. The returned matrix has fit, lwr and upr columns.

Complete local R example; the app itself does not execute it:
```r
data <- data.frame(x = 1:5, y = c(2, 4, 5, 4, 5))
fit <- lm(y ~ x, data = data)
point <- data.frame(x = 3)
mean_interval <- predict(fit, point, interval = "confidence")
chosen <- predict(fit, point, interval = "confidence")
width <- function(x) x[1, "upr"] - x[1, "lwr"]
cat(width(chosen) > width(mean_interval), "\n", sep = "")

```
Expected output or behavior: FALSE. Compiler evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.

Optional local transfer task: Explain why a returned interval at x = 100 would not establish credible extrapolation. You may trace it without a R interpreter; reading completion is not proof of a local run.

At x=3 this range describes uncertainty in the fitted mean. Predicting one new value also needs room for individual variation.

Follow the labeled parts of this example.
```r
data <- data.frame(x = 1:5, y = c(2, 4, 5, 4, 5))
fit <- lm(y ~ x, data = data)
point <- data.frame(x = 3)
mean_interval <- predict(fit, point, interval = "confidence")
chosen <- predict(fit, point, interval = "confidence")
width <- function(x) x[1, "upr"] - x[1, "lwr"]
cat(width(chosen) > width(mean_interval), "\n", sep = "")
```

The output is `FALSE`. Both calls here ask about the same mean, so the second range is not wider. Here x=3 is inside the measured range. A prediction beyond that range depends on the pattern continuing there.

before.question: If chosen uses interval = "prediction", what does the width comparison show?
choices: TRUE; it includes future-observation variation as well as mean uncertainty.
TRUE and it guarantees a future value lies inside.
FALSE because all interval types target the same quantity.
before.explanation: A prediction interval adds residual observation variation, so it is wider for this nonzero-residual fit; it is not a guarantee about any one future outcome.

after.question: At the same x, which range is wider in this example?
choices: The prediction interval for one new value
The confidence interval for the mean
after.explanation: A new observation has extra variation beyond uncertainty in the mean.
